questions.q: A student writes this. What happens when you call f(0)?

options.C: It never reaches the base case and stops with a RecursionError

questions.explain: f(0) calls f(-1), then f(-2), and so on. n moves away from 1, so the base case is never reached. Choose the base case from the smallest input, n == 0 (Notes p.13, p.17).
questions.misconception: The base case is 'the last number you multiply' rather than the smallest input.

options.B: A TypeError: the inner call hands back None because the recursive case never returns

questions.explain: total([3]) computes 3 + 0 but never returns it, so it hands back None. Then total([2, 3]) tries 2 + None and raises a TypeError. Every path that should produce a value needs a return (Notes p.15, p.8).
questions.misconception: Computing a value is the same as returning it.

questions.q: Why does factorial(0) return 1 and not 0?

options.A: Because 0 is not a valid input
options.B: Because Python's math rules say so
options.C: Because multiplying no numbers leaves 1, and a 0 would make every factorial 0 on the way back up

questions.explain: 1 is the do-nothing number for multiplication (the empty product). If factorial(0) returned 0, the 0 would be multiplied into every result while unwinding (Notes p.12).
questions.misconception: The recursion 'ends at 1', so the base case should be 1.
